question: How can we improve an account and judge what sources show?
status: A–F are original factual teaching summaries reused for revision. S1 and S4 are new summaries of two sources studied in Week 2. No historical text, speech, testimony or image is reproduced. The leaflet and court text are not supplied.

campaign_fact_cards.title: A setting and reasons for change
campaign_fact_cards.body: Montgomery bus rules treated Black riders unfairly. These rules had lasted for years. In 1954, the Women’s Political Council asked for fairer bus treatment. Little changed. These grievances gave people reasons to protest.

origin.part: C Unfair bus rules; F Earlier calls for change

campaign_fact_cards.scope: Background and long-term causes. Existing groups enabled action; their existence is not itself the unfair treatment causing protest.
campaign_fact_cards.origin_label: Earlier learning: Week 2 S1; Week 3 C/F.
basis: Week 3 C Unfair bus rules; F Earlier calls for change

campaign_fact_cards.title: An arrest helped set off action
campaign_fact_cards.body: Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on a Montgomery bus. Police arrested her. Organisers then called for people to stay off buses on 5 December. The arrest was a trigger, not the only cause.
campaign_fact_cards.scope: Trigger is distinct from long-term grievances and the later boycott start.
campaign_fact_cards.origin_label: Earlier learning: Week 2 context; Week 3 A; Week 4 B.
basis: Week 4 B A refusal and arrest

campaign_fact_cards.title: Many people sustained the boycott
campaign_fact_cards.body: The boycott began on 5 December 1955. Many Black residents avoided the buses. They walked or shared rides. Volunteers and local groups raised funds and arranged lifts. Shared effort helped the campaign last.

origin.part: S1 A call to stay off buses; S3 Keeping the protest going
C A protest kept going by many

campaign_fact_cards.scope: Do not say every participant used a carpool or one leader sustained the campaign alone.
campaign_fact_cards.origin_label: Earlier learning: Week 2 S1/S3; Week 3 E; Week 4 C.
basis: Week 2 S1 A call to stay off buses; S3 Keeping the protest going
Week 3 E New ways to travel
Week 4 C A protest kept going by many

campaign_fact_cards.title: A separate legal route
campaign_fact_cards.body: Four Black women continued the case Browder v. Gayle. Parks was not a plaintiff. Federal judges ruled against bus segregation on 5 June. The US Supreme Court upheld the ruling on 13 November. Legal action mattered alongside protest.

origin.part: S4 The court ruling and staff note
P1 A legal case alongside the protest
D A separate case changed bus law

campaign_fact_cards.scope: Four plaintiffs continued after an original fifth withdrew; no new claimant names required. The boycott did not itself repeal the law.
campaign_fact_cards.origin_label: Earlier learning: Week 2 S4; Week 3 P1; Week 4 D.
basis: Week 2 S4 The court ruling and staff note
Week 3 P1 A legal case alongside the protest
Week 4 D A separate case changed bus law

campaign_fact_cards.title: The boycott ended and buses changed
campaign_fact_cards.body: After the court order reached Montgomery, the boycott ended on 20 December. People returned to integrated buses on 21 December 1956. The bus seating rule had changed. This did not end racism or every unfair rule.

origin.part: S5 A call to end the boycott and staff check
B A change to bus seating
D A separate case changed bus law

campaign_fact_cards.scope: Distinguish announcement/end on20December from return to integrated buses on21December.
campaign_fact_cards.origin_label: Earlier learning: Week 2 S5; Week 3 B; Week 4 D.
basis: Week 2 S5 A call to end the boycott and staff check
Week 3 B A change to bus seating
Week 4 D A separate case changed bus law

campaign_fact_cards.title: Why the campaign matters
campaign_fact_cards.body: The campaign showed how shared protest could last. Its networks and example helped later civil rights work. Parks’s part mattered, but so did many residents, organisers and the court case. This was one influence among many, not the end of racism.

origin.part: D Links that lasted; G A model for later protests

campaign_fact_cards.scope: Significance needs a reason, not just fame or a list of honours. Do not claim this campaign alone caused every later rights change.
campaign_fact_cards.origin_label: Earlier learning: Week 3 D/G; Week 4 C/D.
basis: Week 3 D Links that lasted; G A model for later protests

review_rows: Where, when, who and unfair rules.
Long grievances and earlier requests; arrest as a trigger.
At least three dated events; shared effort and legal route.
One result by the end and an effect in later years. Explain links.
Why it mattered, with shared work and a limit.
dates_bank: Earlier requests for fairer bus treatment.
Federal court ruling against bus segregation.
US Supreme Court upheld the ruling.
Boycott ended after the court order arrived.
connectives: puts events in order; time alone does not prove a cause
introduces an effect you must explain
adds a limit or a different point
structured_account.requirement: In your book, finish and improve your Week 5 account. Keep all five parts, at least three dated events in order, explained causes and results, the separate legal case, significance and a limit. Retain the earlier draft and show one change with a reason. Then evaluate S1 and S4: what each shows, who made the card and the record or history behind it, how far you trust it for a claim with a reason and limit, and one question it leaves. Keep your own first answers before review.
structured_account.assessment_boundary: Retain the earlier draft and the learner’s revised account, identifying changes and reasons. Retain the first two-source responses before a worked answer or adult reasoning help; record any later supported revision separately.
structured_account.quality: Judge accuracy, structure, explained links, significance and limits. No fixed word count or a longer copy of the model proves the outcome.
structured_account.historical_limit: Many residents and organisers sustained the campaign; Browder v. Gayle was a separate legal route and Parks was not a plaintiff. Changed bus rights did not end racism.

selected_earlier_sources: Week 2 S4 court decisions described in a later history

summaries.title: A first call to stay off buses
summaries.kind: Campaign leaflet described in a new teaching summary
summaries.card_maker: The lesson writer made this summary in 2026.
summaries.record_maker: Members of the Women’s Political Council and local leaders helped make versions of the leaflet.
summaries.purpose: To ask people to join a protest.
summaries.body: Local campaign members prepared and shared a leaflet. It asked Black residents to stay off Montgomery buses on 5 December. The first call was for one day. Later action lasted much longer.
summaries.context_note: The leaflet itself is not supplied. Some date and author details are uncertain. Do not give every version one author.

origin.scope: The call and maker context, not a reproduced leaflet or claim that the first leaflet planned a year.

summaries.staff_strength: Useful evidence of the action organisers asked people to take, in its date and campaign context. Persuasive purpose does not make every claim false.
summaries.staff_limit: A call cannot prove how many joined, what every participant thought or that the planned action happened. Ask for independent records or later checked histories to investigate participation.
summaries.possible_question: How many people joined on the first day, and what independent evidence could check this?
summaries.staff_caution: The earlier source register marked the author and a precise 2 December date as uncertain; keep early December and shared/version authorship. Jo Ann Robinson helped organise preparation, but do not attribute every version solely to her.

summaries.title: Court rulings in a later history
summaries.kind: A later history of court rulings
summaries.card_maker: The lesson writer made this summary in 2026.
summaries.record_maker: Courts made the rulings in 1956. Later, historians at a research institute wrote about them.
summaries.purpose: The court ruled on the law. A later history explains those rulings.
summaries.body: Four Black women continued the case Browder v. Gayle. Judges ruled against bus segregation on 5 June. The US Supreme Court upheld that ruling on 13 November. The legal case worked alongside protest. Parks was not a plaintiff.
summaries.origin_label: Earlier learning: Week 2 S4; Week 3 P1; Week 4 D.
summaries.context_note: The original court text is not supplied. This card describes a later history, checked against another history.

origin.scope: Court decisions described in a later institutional history, not a reproduced court opinion.

summaries.staff_strength: Useful for the legal change, its dates and the separate role of legal action. The claim was checked against another historical account; official status alone does not prove every claim.
summaries.staff_limit: A ruling cannot show every rider’s experience or prove that racism ended. A later summary selects details; check the original decision or other independent evidence for a precise disputed claim.
summaries.possible_question: How did riders’ treatment change after the ruling, and which records could help us check?
summaries.staff_caution: Four plaintiffs continued after an original fifth withdrew. Parks was not a plaintiff. Keep federal ruling 5 June, Supreme Court affirmation 13 November, 20 December boycott end and 21 December integrated bus return distinct.

questions: State one claim this source can support.
Name the teaching-card maker and the maker of the record or history behind it. Use the date and purpose.
Say what claim it helps with, why, and what it cannot show. A maker or purpose alone is not proof.
Ask a real question the source does not settle. Say what other evidence could help.
source_evaluation.authorship_rule: Identify the present teaching-card writer separately from makers of the underlying historical record or later history. A teaching summary is not the original leaflet or court decision.
source_evaluation.trust_rule: Judge a specific claim using maker, date, purpose and checks. Neither persuasive purpose nor official status settles all reliability. State a useful limit and a question left open.

model.status: Original teacher-written guidance; no historical quotation, testimony, image or footage.
model.text: S1 helps us study what organisers asked people to do. It was a call to stay off buses on 5 December. Its campaign purpose makes it useful for that aim. But a call does not count who joined. I would ask how many took part and compare other records. The new card is a summary, not the leaflet itself.
model.note: Review only after both first source answers are retained. This is a newly written teaching explanation, not a source extract or a complete answer to all four questions. Later changes after this model are supported follow-up, not the first assessment response.
